topics.topic: Invocation and attempt identity used for replay
questions: Must the recovered execution use the same pinned versions, exact input, approval, and idempotency key, and is it the same attempt or a new attempt?
For an operation node, must recovery use the identical invocation identity—including the same idempotency key, pinned binding, target and exact input—or create a new execution identity?
For a recovered operation node, must the second invocation use the same target, exact input, pinned binding and idempotency key as the unrecorded invocation, or is it a new invocation with a new key?
Is the recovered execution the same logical execution, a new attempt of the same node execution, or a second node execution, and how are attempts identified in traces and resource accounting?

quotes:
The trace record of one concluded attempt at one node, or of a node that was not
executed because its guards disabled it or an upstream node failed (K-09).

Substitution: an attempt's record is issued once. Continuity: none; a further
attempt is a further record.

On start, before the surface accepts a request, the kernel turns every
`in_flight` EffectAttempt into `unknown` (A11 rule 4) and then derives every
run that has not ended — `running`, `awaiting_approval` or `pending` — again
from its records, oldest first in store order, rewriting a stored status or
waiting point that lags them (a decided approval, a resolved attempt, an
outcome whose run change was lost), and advances, as the
kernel actor, every run that derivation leaves `running`: a
function element without a
concluded record is executed again, which is safe because it has no effect; a `read`
element without one is sent again; an operation element of another class with
neither a concluded record nor an EffectAttempt was never sent and is advanced
as if reached for the first time — an approved, unused approval covers it
only while the rebuilt request has its `request_digest` (A10 rules 1 and 7).
judgement.why: State 1 defines attempt identity, and State 2 distinguishes replayable function/read attempts from effect attempts durably recorded before sending.

topics.topic: Recovery behavior when an effectful operation has an unknown outcome
questions: If an operation may already have produced an effect before its trace write is refused, does recovery execute it again automatically, wait for outcome resolution, or require fresh approval?
After an operation may have produced an effect but its trace could not be stored, must recovery re-invoke it, or must the run wait for the owner's applied/not-applied resolution?

When an effectful operation completed but its trace record was refused, does recovery execute it automatically, or must the run become `outcome_unknown` and wait for the owner's resolution and any required fresh approval?

quotes:
When the kernel cannot tell whether an effect happened, the run rests `pending`
with reason `outcome_unknown` and only the owner's resolution moves it: applied,
or not applied.

An
execution during which the kernel stops because the store refused its record
leaves none, and recovery executes it again.
judgement.divergence: Recovery either invokes the effect again automatically or leaves it pending for owner resolution; the owner and the external service or recipient notice whether a second invocation occurs.
judgement.why: The unconditional recovery instruction conflicts with the rule that an uncertain effect cannot move until the owner resolves it.

Who starts recovery, by what product action, and when: automatically on process restart, through `resume`, or through an operator-only procedure?

quotes:
On start, before the surface accepts a request, the kernel turns every
`in_flight` EffectAttempt into `unknown` (A11 rule 4) and then derives every
run that has not ended — `running`, `awaiting_approval` or `pending` — again
from its records, oldest first in store order, rewriting a stored status or
waiting point that lags them (a decided approval, a resolved attempt, an
outcome whose run change was lost), and advances, as the
kernel actor, every run that derivation leaves `running`:
judgement.why: State 2 makes recovery automatic at process start, performed by the kernel before the surface accepts requests.

topics.topic: Retry policy and terminal state for repeated or permanent trace refusal
questions: What happens if the store refuses the recovered execution's trace record again or remains unavailable indefinitely?
If the store refuses the replacement trace again, how many recovery attempts occur, with what pacing, and what terminal or operator-visible state results?

quotes:
A store failure can leave a run's stored status behind its records. Any
request answered `internal_error` therefore stops the kernel once the
answer is sent, so the next start derives every run (rule 5) before any
request touches one.

| `internal_error` | the failing store change wrote nothing; changes the request made before it stay (Conventions); no detail (A16 rule 7) | the caller re-reads before repeating; the owner reads the host log |
judgement.why: The later rules define one attempt per request or startup recovery, an `internal_error` response and process stop on each store failure, with another recovery only on the next start.

questions: Does "the kernel stops" mean that the process exits, the whole run stops, only the node stops, or the kernel refuses further work while remaining alive?
Does “stops” mean terminating the process, stopping only that node, pausing the run, or refusing all new work, and what observable failure is returned to the caller?
What exactly stops when the trace record is refused: the node, its run, admission of all new work, or the kernel process?

quotes:
If that record cannot be stored,
   the kernel process stops all the same, and recovery executes the element
   again, as it does every function element without a concluded record.

A store failure can leave a run's stored status behind its records. Any
request answered `internal_error` therefore stops the kernel once the
answer is sent, so the next start derives every run (rule 5) before any
request touches one.
judgement.why: State 2 says the kernel process stops, after an `internal_error` answer is sent when the failure occurs during a request.

topics.topic: Visibility, retention, and cleanup of outputs and artifacts from an unrecorded execution
questions: Before the trace record is durably written, may the node's output be stored, exposed to dependants, or handed to a service, and what happens to any output or spool file already produced when the trace write is refused?
Must a trace record be durably accepted before a node's output can be delivered to dependants, or may dependants observe an output from the unrecorded execution?
Must the trace record commit before the node's output can be exposed to downstream nodes or any caller?
Does `leaves none` mean only that no trace exists, or must recovery also discard bounded values, spool files and other kernel artifacts produced by the unrecorded execution before executing it again?

quotes:
A call that fails writes and changes no record; the only
trace it can leave is a published file no record names, which nothing reads:
a spooled file is replaced at its position, value bytes are reused by equal
bytes until the next start removes them (rule 4).

A non-empty list has no
record of its own: the elements' NodeExecutions are its durable facts, and
the list — its StoredValue identity, its files, its class — is derived from
them in element order whenever it is delivered, after a restart too, and
then named by every record that receives it.
judgement.why: State 2 makes concluded records the delivery facts and makes an orphaned file unreadable, replaceable or removable, so an unrecorded output cannot be delivered as a concluded result.

quotes:
Only the store module opens the database. Every change is one call to the
store module and one transaction inside it; callers never open, name or pass a
transaction (K-17). A call that fails writes and changes no record; the only
trace it can leave is a published file no record names, which nothing reads:
a spooled file is replaced at its position, value bytes are reused by equal
bytes until the next start removes them (rule 4).

When a request makes several store changes, those made
before the failed one stay: each is whole, and a run is derived from its
records (A14 rule 6; State 3, "Run state after an element").
judgement.why: Later rules define each store call as its own atomic transaction: the failed change rolls back, earlier completed changes remain, and unreferenced file bytes are not readable results.

topics.topic: Recovery behavior for an unreachable-service wait whose trace was refused
questions: If an execution found its service unreachable and then its trace could not be stored, may recovery retry automatically, or must it reconstruct a pending wait that only resume can continue?

quotes:
An
execution during which the kernel stops because the store refused its record
leaves none, and recovery executes it again.

No wait
ends by itself: a run pending on an unreachable service continues only when the
owner or an agent resumes it; a run pending on an unknown outcome continues only
on the owner's resolution.
judgement.divergence: Recovery either retries the unreachable service automatically or preserves the pending wait until an owner or agent invokes resume; the owner or agent monitoring the run notices when the service is contacted.
judgement.why: The new unconditional recovery sentence conflicts with the existing rule that an unreachable-service wait continues only through resume.

outcomes: Recovery executes the operation again without a resume action.
The run remains pending and the operation is not tried until the owner or an agent resumes it.
witness.observer: The owner or agent monitoring the run and the service
basis:
An operation node invokes one declared
operation of one microservice; only the kernel performs it.

A run
rests `awaiting_approval`, or `pending` when a service is unreachable or an
outcome unknown, and ends `succeeded`, `failed`, `refused` or `cancelled`.

The kernel exposes one fixed set of typed operations over `mcp`: inspect,
author, try, run, resume, read traces, and the owner's approve, accept, activate,
grant, revoke, resolve and cancel.

topics.topic: Retention of exact replay input across the kernel stop
questions: What guarantees that the exact input needed for re-execution, especially a file in the run spool, survives whatever `the kernel stops` means?

quotes:
The data directory holds one SQLite database with every kernel record, a
content-addressed area of value bytes and file fixtures named by digest, and
the run spool, one subdirectory per run.

Everything a resume or a restart needs is in the store before it is acted on:
   records of concluded attempts, decided approvals, and in-flight attempts before
   their request (K-17).
judgement.why: State 2 places the run spool and records in the persistent data directory and requires every restart dependency to be stored before execution.

topics.topic: Store outcomes classified as trace-write refusal
questions: Which store outcomes count as refusal requiring recovery: transient unavailability, transaction conflict, capacity exhaustion, validation failure, an oversized record, or every unsuccessful commit?

topics.topic: Whether replay of an effectful node requires fresh approval
questions: Does recovery re-execution require a fresh approval for an effectful node, and does the answer change for a standing approval?

quotes:
The kernel supplies the declared
idempotency key and never repeats an effect without a fresh approval.

An effect resolved as not applied is sent again only with a fresh
approval, even where a standing approval exists.
judgement.why: State 0 already requires fresh approval for every repeated effect and explicitly says a standing approval does not substitute for it after a not-applied resolution.
